comparison_claims.claim: TULIP-1 (NCT02446899) evaluated anifrolumab in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and missed its primary endpoint of BICLA response at week 52.
The primary endpoint was not met due to insufficient separation between anifrolumab and placebo in the overall population (47.8% vs 31.5%, p=0.06).
The study was underpowered due to higher-than-expected placebo response and lower-than-anticipated treatment effect size.
Post-hoc analysis showed greater benefit in patients with high type I interferon gene signature (IFNS-high), which was not prospectively stratified.
TULIP-2 (NCT02446912), a subsequent phase 3 trial, enriched for IFNS-high patients and met its primary endpoint (BICLA: 47.8% vs 31.5%, p=0.01).
Anifrolumab was later approved by the FDA in 2021 based on TULIP-2 and supportive data from TULIP-1 subgroup analyses.
The IFNS-high biomarker became a key factor in identifying the responsive population for anifrolumab in SLE.
TULIP-1's failure highlighted the importance of biomarker enrichment in SLE trials targeting interferon pathways.
TULIP-1 missed its primary endpoint of SRI-4 response at week 52.
TULIP-1 used a stricter design including a stricter alpha level of 0.05 and considered new NSAID use equivalent to treatment failure, which may have contributed to missing the primary endpoint.
After TULIP-1's failure, investigators evaluated the data and found a more favorable response using BICLA, an alternative measure already collected in the program.
In response to TULIP-1's negative results, investigators in TULIP-2 changed their primary endpoint to BICLA response at week 52.
Unlike SRI, BICLA can capture partial improvements in disease activity.
With the change to BICLA as the primary endpoint, TULIP-2 reached its primary endpoint, showing better BICLA responses in the anifrolumab group than in the placebo group.
TULIP-1 missed its primary endpoint of SRI[4] at Week 52, with a mean difference of -4.2 (95% CI: -14.2 to 5.8) and p-value of 0.412 under the original analysis with restricted medication rules.
